title: Kenyan Kashata
author: Chef Amina Hassan

heritage.origin: Swahili Coast — centuries of Arab and Indian Ocean trade influence
heritage.history: Kashata are traditional Swahili confections made from coconut, groundnuts, or both, cooked in sugar syrup until they set into brittle, sweet clusters. They have been made along the East African coast for centuries, sold at markets, celebrations, and street stalls. The name is believed to derive from Arabic, reflecting the long trade relationship between the Swahili coast and the Arabian Peninsula.
heritage.modernEvolution: Kashata remain one of the most recognisable traditional Swahili sweets, sold in every coastal market and increasingly in Nairobi supermarkets and artisan sweet shops.

desc: Kashata are Kenya's most beloved traditional sweets — coconut and groundnut clusters cooked in a spiced sugar syrup until golden and brittle, with flavours of cardamom and cinnamon. A Swahili coastal confection sold at every market and celebration.
longDesc: Kashata come in two varieties — coconut (kashata ya nazi) and groundnut (kashata ya karanga) — often sold side by side at coastal markets. The sugar syrup is cooked until it reaches the soft crack stage, then the coconut or groundnuts are stirred in and the mixture is spooned onto a greased surface to set. The result is sweet, slightly chewy, fragrant with cardamom, and completely addictive.
ingredients: 2 cups desiccated coconut or roasted groundnuts (or 1 cup each)

substitutions.alternative: Fresh grated coconut — gives a slightly moister result

equipment: Greased baking tray or greased parchment
steps: Grease a baking tray or line with parchment. Set aside.
Combine sugar and water in a heavy saucepan over medium heat.
Stir until sugar dissolves, then stop stirring and allow to boil.
Cook without stirring for 8—10 minutes until the syrup reaches 130°C or forms a soft ball when dropped in cold water.
Add cardamom, cinnamon, salt, vanilla, and butter. Stir quickly.
Add the coconut and/or groundnuts. Stir vigorously to coat everything in the syrup.
Working quickly, spoon heaped tablespoons onto the greased tray.
Flatten slightly with the back of the spoon.
Allow to cool and set completely — about 15—20 minutes.
chefTips: Work very quickly once the nuts or coconut are added — the syrup sets fast.
Have the greased tray ready before you start cooking the syrup.
The soft ball stage (130°C) is critical — too low and they stay sticky; too high and they become too hard.
Wet your hands slightly if you want to shape them by hand instead of spooning.
commonMistakes: Not working fast enough — the mixture sets in the pan.
Sugar syrup too hot — kashata become rock-hard instead of pleasantly chewy.
Not greasing the tray — they stick permanently.

faqs.q: How do I know the syrup is ready without a thermometer?
faqs.a: Drop a small amount into a glass of cold water. If it forms a soft ball that flattens when pressed, it is ready. If it dissolves, cook longer. If it forms a hard ball, it is too hot.

cookingScience: Cooking sugar syrup to the soft ball stage (130°C) produces a supersaturated solution that crystallises around the coconut or nut particles as it cools. The cardamom and cinnamon essential oils are captured in the crystallising sugar matrix, releasing their fragrance with every bite.
sustainabilityTips: Coconut and groundnuts are both widely grown in Kenya — sourcing locally supports farmers.
storage: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.
reheating: Not applicable — serve at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Groundnuts provide plant protein and healthy fats.
Best enjoyed as an occasional treat.
culturalNote: Kashata are among the most recognisable traditional Swahili sweets — present at every coastal market stall, celebration table, and tea break across Kenya. They represent centuries of coastal confectionery tradition.
regionalVariations: Mixed kashata — coconut and groundnut together.
